input: The overrun on the current phase has now grown to 8 weeks, and the principal reason for this disappointing development is the late delivery of a number of long-lead equipment packages that were ordered as part of the EPC scope. These packages were due to arrive well before the installation fronts that depend on them were scheduled to begin, and their late arrival has meant that several fronts have been unable to start on time, with unfortunate knock-on effects right across the sequence of works. It is important to note that work which does not depend on the delayed packages has continued to progress broadly as planned, and every effort is being made to protect the overall completion date. In order to mitigate the impact of the delay, it is proposed that the installation works be resequenced, so that fronts for which all materials are already on site are brought forward, while the delayed fronts absorb the released labour resources as and when their packages finally arrive. Responsibility for delivering this resequencing rests with the EPC contractor, who will report progress against the revised sequence to the project board on a regular basis. While this mitigation cannot recover time on fronts that remain blocked by the outstanding deliveries, it is expected to limit the further growth of the overrun and to make the best possible use of the resources that are currently available on site, although the recovery it can offer is ultimately bounded by the arrival of the packages themselves and by the order in which the completed systems must be handed over for testing.
target: The overrun is now 8 weeks, and the cause sits with the long-lead deliveries under the EPC scope. The packages were due on site before the installation fronts that depend on them were due to start; they arrived after those dates, and the fronts stood idle in sequence. The delay is not spread evenly across the works. Fronts whose materials are on site have continued, and the overrun is confined to the chain of fronts behind the delayed packages, together with the testing and handover steps that follow those fronts. Each blocked front holds the fronts behind it, so the loss grows by accumulation rather than by any single late package. The forecast the board last saw rested on the delivery dates as contracted; the movement since then is a delivery movement, not a change in the scope of the work or in the pace at which the available work is being done, and a further slip in a delivery moves the whole chain behind it. The mitigation is a resequencing of the installation work. Fronts with materials on site move forward and take the labour released by the blocked fronts; the delayed fronts are replanned to start as their packages land, in the order that keeps the commissioning sequence intact. The EPC contractor owns the resequencing and reports progress against the revised sequence to the project board at each review. The resequencing recovers time only where a front can start early without the delayed material and without breaking the order in which systems are handed over for testing. Fronts on the delivery chain keep their dates until the packages arrive, and the recovery the mitigation offers is bounded by that condition. The completion forecast is held open while the resequencing runs, and the board is asked to note the position rather than to approve a revised date on a sequence that has not yet been worked.
